items.answer: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.
The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called the levels of that independent variable or factor.

Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment and are used to design the experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor has two levels, the course's design and MS Word, and these two levels give two test conditions in which text entry speed is observed with each.
Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

questions.question: In experiment design, why should the selected participants be representative of all potential users?
options: To make the conclusions about that user group valid and reliable
To reduce the practice effect in a within-subject design
To make a between-subjects design easier to manage
To ensure the task set covers common interface tasks
questions.explanation: Participants are a subset of all potential users, so if the subset is not representative, the conclusions drawn from it are not valid or reliable.

questions.question: When is it acceptable to use a homogeneous group of experiment participants?
options: When the system is intended for that homogeneous user group
When the system is intended for heterogeneous users
When the task sequence is randomized to reduce practice effects
When the task set is limited to commonly used tasks
questions.explanation: A homogeneous user subset is acceptable when the system is for that homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions about a heterogeneous user group.

questions.question: In experiment design, what is a user profile?
options: The objective data collected while participants perform tasks in the interface
A set of well-defined characteristics used to define the user before selecting participants
The allocation of test conditions to participants in a within-subject design
A small subset of tasks that participants perform during the experiment
questions.explanation: A user profile is a set of well-defined user characteristics; the user is first defined by that profile, and participants are selected only on its basis.

questions.question: Why should age and computer-use frequency be considered when selecting participants for a typing task?
options: Because they indicate whether a random text is representative for the typing task
Because they determine whether a between-subjects design is needed
Because they can lead to different typing behavior and typing speeds
Because they determine how many participants are needed for reliable conclusions
questions.explanation: Older people may have different typing behavior from teenagers, and regular computer users are likely to have different typing speeds from infrequent users.

data.text: Participants must be a representative sample of the whole user group so that the conclusions drawn from the subset are valid. A homogeneous subset is acceptable for a homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous user group. Participants are selected based on a user profile of well-defined characteristics, which must include factors like age and experience that are likely to influence behavior.
points: Participants must be a representative sample of the whole user group for conclusions to be valid.
Homogeneous subsets are only reliable for drawing conclusions if the system is for a homogeneous group.
Participants are selected based on a user profile of well-defined characteristics.
User profiles must include characteristics like age and experience that are likely to influence behavior.

questions.question: In a controlled empirical experiment, why can conclusions from a very small participant group be questionable?
options: They fail because the selected tasks are not representative of the interface.
They may not be reliable and may change if the participant count is increased.
They rely on subjective user preferences instead of task performance data.
They are confounded mainly by a practice effect from repeated practice.
questions.explanation: With a small participant group, the conclusions may be unreliable and can change if the number of participants is increased.

questions.question: In a controlled experiment evaluating an interface, what type of task data is typically collected from users?
options: Mostly system resource usage data.
Mostly user profile characteristics.
Mostly subjective user preference data.
Mostly objective task performance data.
questions.explanation: In such an experiment, users perform tasks, and the collected task performance data are mostly objective.

questions.question: In a controlled interface experiment, why may researchers use only a small subset of all tasks supported by the system?
options: Because random tasks are more reliable for judging usability.
Because subjective data cannot be collected for some tasks.
Because testing all tasks may be limited by time or practicality.
Because each participant must learn the whole system before starting.
questions.explanation: Only a small subset can be used because of less time or practicality, and it must be chosen carefully.

questions.question: What distinguishes a representative task set for an interface from an arbitrary set of tasks?
options: It contains the tasks that potential users most frequently or commonly use in practice.
It is chosen only to minimize the time needed for implementation.
It contains every task supported by the system, regardless of use.
It consists of tasks that are performed by only a few expert users.
questions.explanation: A representative task set is a small, well-defined subset of tasks used by everybody most of the time.

questions.question: When comparing typing interfaces in an experiment, which typing task is representative?
options: A text string selected only for one user profile.
Text strings selected using metrics that indirectly cover the interface and typing skills.
A random piece of text selected from any document.
A text string selected only because it is short.
questions.explanation: A random piece of text is not representative, while representative typing tasks are chosen based on metrics that indirectly encompass the interface and typing skills.

data.text: A participant count between 12 and 25 is generally assumed to be sufficient to draw reliable conclusions in a controlled empirical experiment. Evaluation relies on analyzing objective data collected from users performing specific tasks. Because only a small subset of tasks can be used, these must be chosen carefully from a representative set of tasks that users most frequently use to ensure the data reflects overall usability.
points: A participant count between 12 and 25 is generally assumed to draw reliable conclusions.
Interface evaluation relies on analyzing objective data collected from user tasks.
A representative subset of tasks that users most frequently use must be chosen carefully to ensure the data is useful for drawing reliable conclusions about overall usability.

questions.question: In a between-subjects experimental design, how are the tasks for the test conditions assigned?
options: Every participant performs the tasks corresponding to all test conditions.
They are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.
Tasks are assigned according to participants' user characteristics.
Each participant receives the same numbered task sequence.
questions.explanation: In a between-subjects design, the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.

questions.question: Why may a between-subjects design be selected even when a within-subject design is easier to manage?
options: Because it lets every participant perform all test conditions.
Because it requires the same task sequence for all participants.
Because the availability of participants and resources may force it.
Because it makes the practice effect statistically zero.
questions.explanation: Choosing between within-subject and between-subjects designs depends on circumstances, and participant or resource availability may force a between-subject design.

questions.question: In a within-subject design, what is the practice effect?
options: An improvement in task performance from repeated practice.
A decrease in task performance from repeated practice.
A variation in performance caused by differences in user characteristics.
An improvement in task performance caused by the interface under test.
questions.explanation: The practice effect is an improvement in task performance from repeated practice, and it can confound analysis by making gains appear due to practice rather than the interface.

questions.question: In a within-subject design, how can the practice effect be reduced?
options: By assigning tasks according to participants' user characteristics.
By randomizing or systematically varying the task sequence.
By assigning the same task sequence to every participant.
By selecting only the tasks most commonly used in practice.
questions.explanation: Random or systematic variation of the task sequence is used to nullify the practice effect in a within-subject design.

questions.question: What does a Latin square design do in task assignment?
options: It systematically varies the task sequence by shifting it one position for each successive participant.
It gives the same task sequence to every participant.
It divides the tasks for all conditions among subsets of participants.
It randomly changes the task sequence independently for each participant.
questions.explanation: A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence allocated to each participant, for example by shifting a numbered sequence one position for each successive participant.

data.text: Tasks can be assigned using a within-subject design, where every participant performs all tasks, or a between-subjects design, where tasks are divided among subsets. While within-subject designs are easier to manage, the choice between them depends on participant and resource availability. To reduce the practice effect in within-subject designs, task sequences can be randomized or systematically varied using a Latin square design.
points: Tasks can be assigned using a within-subject design or a between-subjects design.
Within-subject designs are easier to manage, but the choice depends on participant and resource availability.
Repeated practice in a within-subject design can create a practice effect that confounds the analysis.
Randomizing or systematically varying the task sequence can reduce the practice effect.
A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence for each participant.

questions.question: What is the role of the data analysis stage in system implementation?
options: Comparing interfaces using only absolute text-entry speed values
Assigning tasks using a within-subject or between-subjects design
Processing empirical data and testing it for statistical significance before drawing conclusions
Collecting empirical data from the actual population of users
questions.explanation: The data analysis stage is where empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before conclusions about a design's efficacy are drawn.

questions.question: In empirical interface studies, what is the relationship between the data collected and the conclusions of interest?
options: The data come from the actual population, while the conclusions concern the sample of users
The data come from a sample of users, while the conclusions concern the larger population
The data come from one participant, while the conclusions concern the larger population
The data come from the sample of users, while the conclusions concern the sample of users
questions.explanation: Empirical interface studies obtain data from a sample of users, while the conclusions of interest are about the larger population.

questions.question: What does a statistically significant difference between observed data values indicate?
options: It indicates that the participants are the actual population rather than a sample
It indicates that the two groups have exactly the same absolute mean value
It indicates that the difference is not due to chance but to the tested conditions
It indicates that the difference is due to chance rather than the tested conditions
questions.explanation: A statistical significance test shows whether an observed difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a significant difference is not due to chance.

questions.question: When comparing two text-entry interfaces, what does the analysis focus on?
options: The relative difference between the mean text-entry speeds of the groups
The absolute text-entry speed of each individual participant
The practice effect caused by repeated task performance
The number of tasks assigned to each participant
questions.explanation: The analysis uses the mean text-entry speed of each group and concerns the relative difference between those means rather than absolute values.

questions.question: Why is a higher mean text-entry speed by itself not enough to conclude that one interface is better?
options: The higher mean may be due to chance, so a statistically significant difference is required
The higher mean may be due to the tested conditions, so no significance test is required
The higher mean may be due to a randomized task sequence, so a longer experiment is required
The higher mean may be due to chance, so an absolute mean comparison is required
questions.explanation: A higher mean alone may be due to chance; a statistically significant difference between the means is needed to conclude that one design is better in speed or efficiency.

data.text: Empirical data must be tested for statistical significance in the data analysis stage because observed results may be due to chance. These tests show whether differences are reliable for a larger population rather than just a sample. To conclude one design is better than another, there must be a statistically significant difference between the means of the groups.
points: Empirical data must be tested for statistical significance in the data analysis stage before drawing conclusions.
Results from a sample of users are used to draw conclusions about a larger population.
Direct conclusions can be misleading because observed results may be due to chance.
Statistical significance tests show whether differences are reliable or due to chance.
A statistically significant difference between the means of groups is required to conclude one design is better than another.

activities.title: Order the steps of experimental data analysis

items.title: Order the steps of experimental data analysis
steps: Data are tested for statistical significance
Conclusions about the design are drawn

questions.question: What determines which statistical significance test should be selected for an experiment?
options: The nature of the input data and the size of the observed difference
The design of the experiment and the number of participants
The design of the experiment and the nature of the input data
The number of participants and the availability of resources
questions.explanation: The method for performing a statistical significance test depends on the design of the experiment and the nature of the input data.

questions.question: In a statistical significance test, what is the p-value?
options: The probability that the tested conditions are true
The absolute difference between the group means
The probability of obtaining the data by chance
The probability that the observed result is practically important
questions.explanation: The p-value is the probability of obtaining the data by chance, and a lower p-value means the result is less likely to have been obtained by chance.

questions.question: For an experimental design with one factor having two levels, which parametric test is used for a within-subject design?
options: One-way analysis of variance
Paired sample t-test
Independent samples t-test
Repeated measures analysis of variance
questions.explanation: For an experimental design with one factor having two levels, a within-subject design can use the parametric paired sample t-test.

questions.question: For a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels, which parametric test is used?
options: Factorial analysis of variance
Independent samples t-test
Repeated measures analysis of variance
One-way analysis of variance
questions.explanation: For between-subject designs, one-way analysis of variance is used for one factor with more than two levels.

questions.question: For a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels, which non-parametric test can be used?
options: Friedman test
Kruskal-Wallis test
McNemar's test
Mann-Whitney U test
questions.explanation: For a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels, the non-parametric Friedman test can be used.

data.text: The method for performing a statistical significance test depends on the design of the experiment and the nature of the input data. Statistical significance tests fall into two groups: parametric tests and non-parametric tests. Depending on the design, scale of measurement, and number of factors or levels, specific parametric or non-parametric tests can be used.
points: The method for performing a statistical significance test depends on the design of the experiment and the nature of the input data.
Statistical significance tests fall into two groups: parametric tests and non-parametric tests.
For a nominal scale of measurement and one factor with two levels, specific non-parametric tests are used.
For designs with one factor and two levels, specific parametric or non-parametric tests can be used.
For designs with more factors or levels, various parametric and non-parametric tests can be used.

questions.question: Why must both the participants and the tasks in an empirical interface study be representative of real users and real use?
questions.reference_answer: Participants are a sample of the whole user group, so if the sample is not representative, the conclusions drawn from the experiment are not valid or reliable. The experiment can use only a small subset of all tasks, so it should choose from the representative task set of tasks that users commonly use; otherwise the observed data may not support a reliable conclusion about the overall usability of the interface.

questions.question: When comparing two text-entry interfaces, why is a statistically significant difference between mean text-entry speeds required rather than simply noticing that one mean is higher?
questions.reference_answer: A straightforward conclusion from experimental data can be misleading because an observed data difference may be due to chance, and changing the participants or conditions may produce different data and a different conclusion. A statistical significance test indicates whether the observed data difference is reliable by showing whether it is due to chance or to the tested conditions. Therefore, a higher mean text-entry speed alone is not enough; a statistically significant difference is required to conclude that one text-entry interface is better in speed or efficiency.

questions.question: What is one practical reason to prefer a within-subject design, and what method can be used to reduce its main confounding effect?
questions.reference_answer: In a within-subject design every participant performs the tasks for all test conditions, while a between-subjects design divides the tasks for all test conditions among different participants, so within-subject designs are easier to manage. Repeated practice can improve task performance, creating a practice effect that is a confounding variable and may be mistaken for an effect of the interface. To reduce this effect, the task sequence can be randomized or systematically varied, for example by using a Latin square design, and these variations are supposed to nullify the practice effect.

questions.question: How does data analysis in stage 4 of the system implementation process support a conclusive usability assessment of a fully implemented system?
questions.reference_answer: Data analysis is stage 4 of the system implementation process, where empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before conclusions are drawn about a design, such as text entry speed. A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data. For a text entry speed question, the experiment can collect objective data by having all users input the same text and logging speed as characters per minute. This allows data analysis to turn objective behavioral data from the implemented system into evidence for a usability judgment.
